::: {.lead}
A mining game stores its level as a table: in each tile, the number of gems.
An RPG stores its enemies as a table: one row for each enemy, one column for
each stat. A puzzle game moves a crystal with spells, and each spell is a
small table of numbers. All these tables are **matrices**. In this lesson
you learn to read a matrix, to add it and multiply it by a number, and to
multiply it with a position: the first step towards the transformations of
the next lectures. Every section ends with a short task.
:::

## Key terms

{{< glossary matrix matrix-row matrix-column matrix-size matrix-entry matrix-addition column-vector matrix-multiplication commutative identity-matrix inverse-matrix square-matrix main-diagonal >}}

## 5.1 The mine map: what a matrix is

The level designer of a mining game draws a mine of 3 rows of 4 tiles. Each tile
holds some gems. The programmer needs one name for the whole map, and a clear
way to say "the tile in row 2, column 3". A matrix gives both (@fig-map).

::: {.callout-important title="Definition 5.1 — Matrix, size and entry"}
A **matrix** is a rectangular table of numbers in **rows** (across) and
**columns** (down). Its **size** is "rows × columns": a matrix with 3 rows and
4 columns is a 3 × 4 matrix. The number in row *i* and column *j* is the
**entry** $a_{ij}$. The row number always comes first.
:::

![The gem map of a mining game as a 3 × 4 matrix M. The entry $m_{23}$ (row 2, column 3) is 0.](images/matrix-map.png){#fig-map width=96%}

$$M = \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 0 & 5 & 1 \\ 4 & 3 & 0 & 6 \\ 1 & 7 & 2 & 0 \end{bmatrix}$$

Matrices are written with a capital letter (M, A, B), and their entries with
the small letter and two numbers: $m_{23}$ is "m two three", not "m
twenty-three".

::: {.callout-note title="Example 5.1 — Reading the mine map"}
1. M has 3 rows and 4 columns, so its size is **3 × 4**. It has 3 × 4 = 12
   entries.
2. $m_{14}$ is in row 1, column 4: **1** gem.
3. $m_{32}$ is in row 3, column 2: **7** gems. $m_{23}$ is in row 2, column 3:
   **0** gems. Swapping the two numbers gives another tile.
:::

::: {.callout-warning title="Common mistake"}
Writing the size as "columns × rows". The size of M is 3 × 4, not 4 × 3. A
spreadsheet makes this mistake easy: the cell C2 is column C, row 2, but the
entry $a_{23}$ is row 2, column 3.
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Do it · Your own level as a matrix"}
On squared paper, draw a small level of 3 rows and 3 tiles. Write a number of
coins in each tile.

1. Write the level as a matrix L. What is its size?
2. Circle $l_{32}$ and $l_{23}$. Are they the same tile?

*Your result:* the matrix L, its size, and the two circled entries.

::: {.check}
L is a 3 × 3 matrix. $l_{32}$ is row 3, column 2 and $l_{23}$ is row 2,
column 3: two different tiles (unless their numbers happen to be equal).
:::
:::

## 5.2 Two rounds, one total: adding and scaling matrices

A puzzle game shows the points of two players (rows) in three levels
(columns). Round 1 gives one matrix of points, the bonus round another. The
total of each player in each level is the sum of two entries in the same
place (@fig-add).

::: {.callout-important title="Definition 5.2 — Matrix addition and subtraction"}
Two matrices of the **same size** are added entry by entry:
$(A + B)_{ij} = a_{ij} + b_{ij}$. Subtraction works the same way:
$(A - B)_{ij} = a_{ij} - b_{ij}$. The result has the same size. Matrices of
different sizes cannot be added.
:::

![Adding two 2 × 3 matrices: every entry with the entry in the same place.](images/matrix-add.png){#fig-add width=96%}

::: {.callout-note title="Example 5.2 — Points after the bonus round"}
$$\begin{bmatrix} 120 & 80 & 50 \\ 90 & 60 & 40 \end{bmatrix} + \begin{bmatrix} 30 & 20 & 10 \\ 10 & 40 & 0 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 150 & 100 & 60 \\ 100 & 100 & 40 \end{bmatrix}$$

1. Both matrices are 2 × 3, so the sum exists and is 2 × 3.
2. Player 1 in level 2: 80 + 20 = 100.
3. Player 2 in level 3: 40 + 0 = 40.
:::

::: {.callout-warning title="Common mistake"}
Adding a 2 × 3 matrix to a 3 × 2 matrix. There is no entry in the same place
for every number, so the sum does not exist. Check the sizes first.
:::

{{< sim file="sims/matrix-lab.html" poster="sims/matrix-lab.png" title="Matrix Lab: add, subtract and multiply by a number" height="560" >}}

### Hard mode: multiplying a matrix by a number

In hard mode, every enemy of an RPG has 1.5 times its HP, damage and speed.
The enemy table E has one row per enemy (slime, troll) and the columns HP,
damage and speed.
The designer does not change the table number by number: the game multiplies
the whole matrix by 1.5 (@fig-scale).

::: {.callout-important title="Definition 5.3 — A number times a matrix"}
To multiply a matrix A by a number k (a **scalar**), multiply every entry by
k: $(kA)_{ij} = k\,a_{ij}$. The size does not change.
:::

![Hard mode multiplies every entry of the stats matrix by 1.5.](images/matrix-scale.png){#fig-scale width=96%}

::: {.callout-note title="Example 5.3 — The stats in hard mode"}
$$1.5 \begin{bmatrix} 40 & 10 & 4 \\ 60 & 20 & 2 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 60 & 15 & 6 \\ 90 & 30 & 3 \end{bmatrix}$$

1. The troll's HP: 1.5 × 60 = 90.
2. The slime's damage: 1.5 × 10 = 15.
:::

::: {.callout-warning title="Common mistake"}
Multiplying only one row or one column. The number multiplies **every** entry
of the matrix.
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Do it · Add and scale in Matrix Lab"}
Open **Matrix Lab** (above, or scan the QR code). Choose A + B and tap one
entry of the result. Then choose k × A.

1. Set k = 1.5 and tap two entries of the result. Write each product.
2. Set k = −1. What happens to every sign?

*Your result:* one sum, two products and one sentence about k = −1.

::: {.check}
A sum: the two entries in the same place added. With k = 1.5 every entry is
1.5 times bigger (for example 1.5 × 4 = 6). With k = −1 every sign changes.
:::
:::

## 5.3 Casting a spell: a matrix times a vector

The crystal of *Crystal Spells* stands at (4, 1). The spell "Stretch" doubles
x and triples y. The game keeps the spell as a 2 × 2 matrix and the position
as a column vector, and multiplies them (@fig-mv).

::: {.callout-important title="Definition 5.4 — Matrix times vector"}
To multiply a matrix A by a column vector **v**, take each **row** of A times
**v**: multiply the pairs of numbers and add them. This is the dot product of
Lecture 2. For a 2 × 2 matrix:
$$\begin{bmatrix} a & b \\ c & d \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} x \\ y \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} ax + by \\ cx + dy \end{bmatrix}$$
:::

![Each row of the matrix times the vector gives one coordinate. The point (4, 1) goes to (8, 3).](images/matrix-vector.png){#fig-mv width=96%}

::: {.callout-note title="Example 5.4 — The spell Stretch"}
$$\begin{bmatrix} 2 & 0 \\ 0 & 3 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} 4 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 2 \times 4 + 0 \times 1 \\ 0 \times 4 + 3 \times 1 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 8 \\ 3 \end{bmatrix}$$

1. Row 1 times the vector gives the new x: 8.
2. Row 2 times the vector gives the new y: 3.
3. The crystal moves from (4, 1) to (8, 3).
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Example 5.5 — The spell Turn"}
Turn has the rows (0, −1) and (1, 0). The crystal stands at (3, 2).

1. Row 1: 0 × 3 + (−1) × 2 = −2.
2. Row 2: 1 × 3 + 0 × 2 = 3.
3. The crystal goes to (−2, 3): (x, y) became (−y, x), a turn of 90°
   anticlockwise. Lecture 6 explains why.
:::

A 2 × 2 matrix times a 2 × 1 vector gives a 2 × 1 vector: the result is
again a position. One matrix can move every point of a sprite in the same
way: this is how games apply a transformation.

::: {.callout-warning title="Common mistake"}
Multiplying entry by entry: 2 × 4 and 3 × 1 only. Every row uses **both**
coordinates: 0 × 4 + 3 × 1. The zeros matter in other matrices.
:::

{{< sim file="sims/multiply-lab.html" poster="sims/multiply-lab.png" title="Multiply Lab: a 2 × 2 matrix moves a point and a shape" height="760" >}}

::: {.callout-note title="Do it · Check Turn in Multiply Lab"}
Open **Multiply Lab** (above, or scan the QR code).

1. On paper, multiply Turn (rows (0, −1) and (1, 0)) by P = (2, 3).
2. In the lab, press "Turn 90°" and drag P to (2, 3). Compare.

*Your result:* your two rows of calculation and the point from the lab.

::: {.check}
Row 1: 0 × 2 + (−1) × 3 = −3. Row 2: 1 × 2 + 0 × 3 = 2. Turn sends (2, 3) to
(−3, 2); the lab shows the same point.
:::
:::

### Two spells at once: a matrix times a matrix

A model of 2000 points gets two spells in a row. The game does not multiply
every point twice. It multiplies the two matrices **once** and uses the
result for every point. So we need the product of two matrices (@fig-mm).

::: {.callout-important title="Definition 5.5 — Matrix times matrix"}
The product AB exists when A has as many **columns** as B has **rows**. If A
is m × n and B is n × p, then AB is m × p. Its entry in row *i*, column *j*
is row *i* of A times column *j* of B (a dot product).
:::

![The entry in row 1, column 2 of AB is row 1 of A times column 2 of B.](images/matrix-matrix.png){#fig-mm width=96%}

::: {.callout-note title="Example 5.6 — Four dot products"}
A has the rows (1, 2) and (3, 0); B has the rows (4, 1) and (0, 2).

1. Row 1 · column 1: 1 × 4 + 2 × 0 = 4. Row 1 · column 2: 1 × 1 + 2 × 2 = 5.
2. Row 2 · column 1: 3 × 4 + 0 × 0 = 12. Row 2 · column 2: 3 × 1 + 0 × 2 = 3.
3. $AB = \begin{bmatrix} 4 & 5 \\ 12 & 3 \end{bmatrix}$.
:::

::: {.callout-warning title="Common mistake"}
Multiplying entry by entry, as in addition: 1 × 4, 2 × 1, …. That is not the
matrix product. Each entry of AB is a whole row times a whole column.
:::

## 5.4 First stretch, then turn: the order matters

A level designer stretches a platform to double width and then turns it by
90°. A second designer turns first and stretches after. Their platforms are
not the same (@fig-order). With numbers, AB and BA usually differ.

::: {.callout-important title="Definition 5.6 — Not commutative"}
Matrix multiplication is **not commutative**: in general $AB \neq BA$. In
$AB\mathbf{v}$, the matrix next to the vector acts first: first B, then A.
Read a product of transformations from **right to left**.
:::

![Stretch then turn (left) and turn then stretch (right) give different shapes.](images/order-matters.png){#fig-order width=96%}

::: {.callout-note title="Example 5.7 — AB and BA"}
With A and B of Example 5.6:

1. $BA$: row 1 of B times the columns of A: 4 × 1 + 1 × 3 = 7 and
   4 × 2 + 1 × 0 = 8.
2. Row 2 of B: 0 × 1 + 2 × 3 = 6 and 0 × 2 + 2 × 0 = 0.
3. $BA = \begin{bmatrix} 7 & 8 \\ 6 & 0 \end{bmatrix}$, but
   $AB = \begin{bmatrix} 4 & 5 \\ 12 & 3 \end{bmatrix}$.
:::

::: {.callout-warning title="Common mistake"}
Reading a product from left to right. In $AB\mathbf{v}$, B acts first.
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Do it · Order on paper and in the lab"}
Flip has the rows (−1, 0) and (0, 1); Turn has the rows (0, −1) and (1, 0).
Take the point (3, 1).

1. On paper, apply Flip then Turn, and Turn then Flip.
2. In **Multiply Lab**, put P at (3, 1). Press "Flip x" and read MP. Then
   enter that point as P, press "Turn 90°", and read MP again.

*Your result:* the two end points, and which order the lab followed.

::: {.check}
Flip then Turn: (3, 1) → (−3, 1) → (−1, −3). Turn then Flip: (3, 1) →
(−1, 3) → (1, 3). Two different points: the order matters. The lab followed
Flip first, then Turn.
:::
:::

## 5.5 The spell that changes nothing: the identity

A new object in a scene stands at the origin, is not turned and has size 1.
Its matrix must change nothing. This matrix is the **identity** (@fig-id).

::: {.callout-important title="Definition 5.7 — Identity matrix"}
The **identity matrix** I is the square matrix with 1 on the main diagonal
and 0 everywhere else. For every matrix A and vector **v** of matching size:
$IA = AI = A$ and $I\mathbf{v} = \mathbf{v}$.
:::

![The identity matrix leaves every point where it is.](images/identity.png){#fig-id width=96%}

::: {.callout-note title="Example 5.8 — I times a point"}
$$\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} 5 \\ -2 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 \times 5 + 0 \times (-2) \\ 0 \times 5 + 1 \times (-2) \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 5 \\ -2 \end{bmatrix}$$

1. The 1 in row 1 keeps x; the 0 removes y from the new x.
2. The 1 in row 2 keeps y. The point stays at (5, −2).
:::

::: {.callout-warning title="Common mistake"}
Thinking that a matrix of 1s is the identity. The matrix with the rows (1, 1)
and (1, 1) sends (5, −2) to (3, 3). The identity has 1s only on the main
diagonal.
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Do it · The identity in Multiply Lab"}
In **Multiply Lab**, press "Identity".

1. Drag P to three different points. Where is MP each time?
2. Change one 0 into a 1. What happens to the house?

*Your result:* three points and one sentence about the change.

::: {.check}
With the identity, MP is always the same as P. When a 0 becomes 1, a
coordinate is added to the other one, so the house leans: it is no longer
the identity.
:::
:::

## 5.6 Undo: the inverse matrix

The player casts Grow by mistake: the crystal jumps from (3, 2) to (6, 4).
The game needs the spell that brings it back. This is the **inverse** of
Grow (@fig-inv).

::: {.callout-important title="Definition 5.8 — Inverse"}
The **inverse** of a square matrix A is the matrix $A^{-1}$ that undoes it:
$AA^{-1} = A^{-1}A = I$. Doing A and then $A^{-1}$ (or the other way round)
changes nothing.
:::

![Grow takes P = (3, 2) to (6, 4); its inverse brings it back.](images/inverse.png){#fig-inv width=96%}

::: {.callout-note title="Example 5.9 — Undo Grow"}
Grow has the rows (2, 0) and (0, 2): it doubles x and y.

1. To undo it, halve x and y: the rows (0.5, 0) and (0, 0.5). This is
   Shrink.
2. Check: Shrink × (6, 4) = (0.5 × 6, 0.5 × 4) = (3, 2). The crystal is back.
3. Shrink × Grow = I: the two spells together change nothing.
:::

Not every spell can be undone. Squash has the rows (1, 2) and (1, 2): it
sends both (2, 0) and (0, 1) to the same point (2, 2). From (2, 2), no spell
can know which point came first, so Squash has **no inverse**.

::: {.callout-warning title="Common mistake"}
Thinking that every matrix has an inverse, or that the inverse is "1 ÷ every
entry". A spell that sends two points to the same place cannot be undone.
Always check: $A^{-1}A$ must give the identity.
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Do it · Undo in Multiply Lab"}
In **Multiply Lab**:

1. Press "Grow" and drag P to (2, 1). Write MP. Then enter the rows
   (0.5, 0) and (0, 0.5) and put P at that point. Where does it go?
2. Press "Squash" and look at the house. Why can it not come back?

*Your result:* the two points and one sentence about Squash.

::: {.check}
Grow sends (2, 1) to (4, 2); Shrink brings (4, 2) back to (2, 1). Squash
puts the whole house on one line: many points land on the same place, so no
spell can bring them back.
:::
:::

## Case study: Crystal Spells

*Crystal Spells* is a made-up puzzle game. The crystal starts at (2, 1).
Each spell is a 2 × 2 matrix: **Grow** = rows (2, 0) and (0, 2); **Shrink** =
rows (0.5, 0) and (0, 0.5); **Turn** = rows (0, −1) and (1, 0); **Flip** =
rows (−1, 0) and (0, 1); **Stay** = the identity. The player must predict
where a spell sends the crystal, choose the spell for a gate, keep the
crystal still on a trap, and undo a mistake. The Game challenge of the
interactive lesson uses these numbers. In the mini-game below you play five
rounds.

{{< sim file="sims/crystal-spells.html" poster="sims/crystal-spells.png" title="Crystal Spells: cast the right matrix" kind="game" height="720" >}}

## Further reading

Dunn and Parberry, *3D Math Primer for Graphics and Game Development*,
2nd ed., Chapter 4 (matrices: notation, multiplying matrices, the identity)
and Chapter 6 (the idea of the inverse).

## Exercises

1. A matrix has 2 rows and 5 columns. What is its size, and how many entries
   does it have?
2. In the mine map M, what is $m_{21}$? What is $m_{12}$?
3. Add the matrices with rows (3, 1), (0, 2) and rows (1, 1), (4, −2).
4. Can a 3 × 2 matrix and a 2 × 3 matrix be added? Why?
5. Compute 3A for A with rows (2, 0) and (−1, 4).
6. Multiply the rows (3, 0) and (0, 1) by the vector (2, 5).
7. Multiply the rows (1, 2) and (0, 1) by the vector (1, 3).
8. A is 3 × 2 and B is 2 × 5. Does AB exist? What is its size? Does BA
   exist?
9. Compute AB for A = rows (1, 1), (0, 2) and B = rows (3, 0), (1, 1).
10. Compute BA for the same A and B. Is it equal to AB?
11. In $AB\mathbf{v}$, which matrix acts first on **v**?
12. What is I × (7, −3)?
13. Grow3 has the rows (3, 0) and (0, 3). Which matrix undoes it?
14. *Crystal Spells*: the crystal is at (2, 1). Which spell sends it to
    (−2, 1)? Which spell undoes Grow?

## Answers to the exercises

::: {.answers}
1. 2 × 5; 10 entries.
2. $m_{21} = 4$; $m_{12} = 0$.
3. Rows (4, 2) and (4, 0).
4. No: the sizes are different.
5. Rows (6, 0) and (−3, 12).
6. (6, 5).
7. (1 + 6, 0 + 3) = (7, 3).
8. Yes, 3 × 5. BA: (2 × 5) times (3 × 2): 5 and 3 differ, so no.
9. Rows (4, 1) and (2, 2).
10. Rows (3, 3) and (1, 3). No: AB ≠ BA.
11. B, the matrix next to the vector.
12. (7, −3).
13. The rows (1/3, 0) and (0, 1/3): it divides x and y by 3.
14. Flip. Shrink.
:::
